subject: anatomy
title: Palatine Tonsil, Tonsillar Bed, Quinsy, and Zenker Diverticulum

steps.tx: The palatine tonsils are two prominent almond-shaped lymphoid masses situated bilaterally in the lateral wall of the oropharynx. Each **palatine tonsil** is nestled within the tonsillar sinus (tonsillar fossa), bounded anteriorly by the palatoglossal arch (anterior pillar) and posteriorly by the palatopharyngeal arch (posterior pillar).
steps.say: The palatine tonsils reside in the lateral oropharynx between the palatoglossal arch anteriorly and the palatopharyngeal arch posteriorly, forming part of Waldeyer ring.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram of the palatine tonsil showing tonsillar crypts, pillars, and tonsillar bed relations
vis.caption: Anatomical relationships of the palatine tonsil within the tonsillar bed and surrounding muscular pillars. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: The palatine tonsils form the lateral components of Waldeyer lymphoid ring, a protective annular defensive ring of mucosal lymphoid tissue guarding the respiratory and alimentary entrances. **Waldeyer ring** is constituted by the pharyngeal tonsil (adenoids) superiorly, the tubal tonsils dorsolaterally, the palatine tonsils laterally, and the lingual tonsil inferiorly on the posterior third of the tongue.
steps.say: Waldeyer ring guards the pharyngeal gateway. It is formed by the adenoids superiorly, tubal tonsils laterally, palatine tonsils intermediately, and the lingual tonsil inferiorly.

nodes.label: Superior: Pharyngeal Tonsil (Adenoids in nasopharyngeal roof)
Dorsolateral: Tubal Tonsils (Mucosa around Eustachian tube orifices)
Lateral: Palatine Tonsils (Bilateral masses in tonsillar sinuses)
Inferior: Lingual Tonsil (Lymphoid follicles on posterior third of tongue)

steps.tx: The medial free surface of the palatine tonsil is covered by non-keratinised stratified squamous epithelium, deeply pitted by twelve to fifteen tonsillar crypts. The largest crypt near the upper pole is designated the **crypta magna** (intratonsillar cleft), representing the embryonic remnant of the second pharyngeal pouch. Food debris and bacterial casts characteristically collect within these crypts.
steps.say: Twelve to fifteen tonsillar crypts invaginate the medial surface. The largest, crypta magna near the upper pole, represents the embryonic second pharyngeal pouch.

left.title: Medial Surface of Tonsil
points: Projects freely into the oropharyngeal lumen
Covered by stratified squamous non-keratinised epithelium
Invaginated by 12 to 15 branching tonsillar crypts
Crypta magna houses cellular debris and tonsilloliths

right.title: Lateral Surface of Tonsil
points: Invested by a distinct dense fibrous hemicapsule
Separated from pharyngeal wall by loose areolar cleft
Crossed by paratonsillar vein and tonsillar artery

steps.tx: The tonsillar bed forms the deep lateral relation of the tonsil, constructed primarily by the superior constrictor muscle and the hyoglossus. Covering the outer surface of the tonsil is a distinct fibrous **hemicapsule**, separated from the superior constrictor by loose areolar tissue (the peritonsillar space). This loose cleft provides the standard cleavage plane during surgical tonsillectomy.
steps.say: The tonsillar bed consists of the superior constrictor muscle. A loose areolar peritonsillar space separates the tonsil capsule from the bed, guiding dissection in tonsillectomy.

nodes.label: Palatine Tonsil Parenchyma (Lymphoid follicles with germinal centres)
Fibrous Hemicapsule (Dense specialized layer covering lateral surface)
Peritonsillar Space (Loose areolar cleavage plane containing paratonsillar vein)
Tonsillar Bed (Superior constrictor muscle and pharyngobasilar fascia)

steps.tx: The blood supply to the palatine tonsil is exceptionally abundant, derived from five arterial branches. The chief arterial feeder is the tonsillar branch of the **facial artery**, which enters the lower pole of the gland. Additional contributions derive from the ascending palatine (facial), ascending pharyngeal (ECA), dorsal lingual (lingual), and greater palatine (maxillary) arteries.
steps.say: Five arteries feed the tonsil, led by the tonsillar branch of the facial artery at the lower pole. Dorsal lingual, ascending pharyngeal, and palatine branches also contribute.

rows: Pierces superior constrictor to enter inferior pole
Enters upper pole of tonsil alongside levator palati
Supplies anterior lower border and lingual tonsil
Ascends on pharyngeal wall to enter posterolateral surface
Descends through palatine canal to supply superior pole

steps.tx: A severe acute complication of tonsillitis is the development of a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy). Pus breaks through the tonsillar capsule into the loose areolar peritonsillar space. The expanding **quinsy** displaces the palatine tonsil medially and downward, pushes the oedematous uvula across the midline to the opposite side, and causes excruciating sore throat, severe trismus, and a hot-potato voice.
steps.say: A peritonsillar abscess develops when infection escapes the capsule into the peritonsillar space. The tonsil is displaced medially, the uvula deviates, and trismus develops.

left.title: Severe Acute Tonsillitis
points: Uvula remains centered in the midline

right.title: Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy)
points: Unilateral fluctuant bulging above tonsillar pole
Uvula pushed across to contralateral side
Severe trismus due to pterygoid muscle irritation

steps.tx: During tonsillectomy, secondary haemorrhage most commonly arises from the paratonsillar vein (external palatine vein). Descending from the soft palate across the loose peritonsillar space, the **paratonsillar vein** is severed during capsular dissection. Venous bleeding can be copious and demands careful bipolar diathermy or suturing of the tonsillar pillars.
steps.say: The paratonsillar vein traverses the loose peritonsillar cleft. Severed during capsular dissection, it represents the most frequent culprit behind post-tonsillectomy haemorrhage.

nodes.label: Soft Palate Venous Plexus (Descends across loose peritonsillar space)
Paratonsillar Vein (Crosses lateral surface of tonsillar hemicapsule)
Pharyngeal Venous Plexus (Pierces superior constrictor to drain into IJV)
Operative Bleeding (Traction during dissection tears vein in the bed)

steps.tx: At the junction of the laryngopharynx and oesophagus, the inferior constrictor muscle is divided into an upper oblique thyropharyngeus and a lower horizontal cricopharyngeus. Between these two muscular parts lies a potential triangular weakness designated **Killian dehiscence**. Elevated intraluminal pressure causes the mucosal lining to herniate posteriorly through this gap, forming a Zenker diverticulum.
steps.say: Killian dehiscence is a potential triangular weak spot between the thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus muscles. Mucosal herniation through this gap produces a Zenker diverticulum.
